children: Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni's party has proposed scaling back a disputed "exit tax" on wealthy individuals leaving the country by limiting it to those moving to tax havens, parliamentary documents showed.
The planned levy, part of next year's budget currently before parliament, triggered wide-spread criticism from tax experts and wealth advisers, who said it would hamper Italy's appeal for investors.

In its current form, the tax envisages a 26% levy on the unrealised capital gains of individuals holding financial investments worth at least €800,000 ($878,800.00) who ​transfer their tax domicile abroad.

Ylenja Lucaselli, a lawmaker from Meloni's Brothers of Italy party, has tabled an amendment that would replace the €800,000 threshold with one of at least €2 million in total income stemming for the assets.

Moreover, the tax would only be due if the individual moves to a country "where the effective tax rate is zero or less than 1% and which does not ensure an adequate exchange of tax information with Italy," the text of the amendment shows.
The levy would apply to transfers made by someone who has spent at least eight of the last 10 fiscal years in Italy, up from the six years under the government's proposal.
Government officials said the cabinet office was looking favourably at Lucaselli's proposal, which could be adopted fully or in part.

Another proposal, tabled by the co-ruling Forza Italia party, aims to €5 million euros the investment threshold that would trigger the levy, while other ruling lawmakers are pushing to cancel the tax altogether.
The debate comes amid growing wealth concentration among top earners in Italy and stagnant real wages for low- and middle-income workers.
Data from the Bank of Italy's most recent household budget survey showed that the bottom 10% of earners received 2.4% of total income in 2022, compared with 27.9% for the top 10%.
The gap between the two shares widened by about 1.6 percentage points from 2020.
The budget must be approved by Parliament by the end of this year to avoid automatic curbs on spending and revenue measures that would otherwise kick in at the start of 2027.
